transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-06-03
Start time (UTC): 16:00
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Carlos Mendes (Nimbus Head of Platform), Amy Wu (ML Eng), Tom Reynolds (Security), Samir Patel (Product)

Auto-generated sections (may be imperfect):
Summary: Quickstart, streaming, retry patterns, PHI constraints, next steps agreed.
Topics: hosted quickstart, streaming resumable chunks, idempotency, latency targets, SOC2/KMS questions.
Action items: see metadata.

Transcript: (timestamps approximate, transcription has errors)
[00:00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone thanks for joining, I'm Jordan with Redwood, and with me is Priya who will run most of the demo, say hi Priya.
[00:00:08] Priya: Hi all, excited to walk through our hosted API quickstart and specifically show streaming behaviors and the retry patterns we recommend.
[00:00:14] Carlos: Thanks, Jordan. Quick note — we're on Pacific, so apologies if we sound groggy. Our main ask today is can hosted meet our latency needs for patient-facing chat, and what the security boundary looks like for PHI.
[00:00:26] Jordan: Totally, and that's exactly what we want to focus on. Quick qualification then demo. Carlos, can you confirm current stack?
[00:00:32] Carlos: Sure. We're running inference in-house with Triton on k8s, mostly grpc endpoints, and we do batching manually. Latency is okay but costs and ops are heavy. Our target for interactive chat is median <80ms and p95 <200ms for short prompts (under 200 tokens). Budget constraint is roughly $X per month — I'll share exact.
[00:00:49] Priya: Got it. That latency target is tight but reachable on hosted with proper model choice and routing — and we can show batching/caching tradeoffs in Optimize. Also need to confirm PHI handling; Tom can speak to the compliance asks.
[00:01:01] Tom: Right — we need HIPAA controls: SOC2 is baseline, but we need KMS-based encryption, audit logs, and optional private deployment if required. Also data residency questions for EU.
[00:01:12] Jordan: We support customer-managed KMS, audit logs, and Private/VPC options. For starting, many customers pilot on Hosted with encryption at rest + access logs, then move to Dedicated/Private if needed.
[00:01:22] Samir: From product we'd like to see behavior for streaming partial answers and how to handle retries cleanly — we don't want duplicated content in the UI.

[00:01:35] Priya: Ok jumping into the console — quick note, I'm using a dev account with a small hosted endpoint. (screen share noises) So quickstart: call the /v1/chat/completions or /v1/generate depending on flow. For streaming we open a server-sent events stream and tokens come as delta chunks.
[00:01:57] Amy: Is streaming chunk size configurable? We saw some vendors stream very small tokens which is chatty.
[00:02:04] Priya: Two levers: model internal chunking and client-side windowing. You can tune the model's response_length and tokenization choices; also we support chunk_aggregation in SDKs (client buffer) so you can group SSE events into larger UI updates. That reduces chattiness at the cost of a little additional latency.
[00:02:22] Jordan: Also important: sending small prompt prefixes repeatedly can be wasteful — prefix caching helps. We can pin conversation contexts to lower latencies.

[00:02:35] [00:02:35] Priya: Demonstrating a simple chat streaming example — prompt: "Schedule a follow-up for patient X — provide brief confirmation." Starting stream... (partial tokens appear)
[00:02:47] Priya: You'll see tokens coming every ~80ms in this region, because the model and hardware match. In our hosted profile this endpoint uses an LLM-faster variant optimized for short-turn latency.
[00:03:01] Amy: That looks good. What happens if the connection resets mid-stream?
[00:03:06] Priya: Good question — we recommend idempotency keys for generation calls. Our client SDK will re-issue with the same idempotency token; the server either returns a cached completed response if available, or resumes a new generation. There is still a small window where you may get duplicate partials; we provide delta-token offsets and top-level generation_id to correlate.
[00:03:27] Carlos: Delta-token offsets? That sounds helpful, can you elaborate?
[00:03:30] Priya: Sure. We include optional metadata on stream events: chunk_index and total_offset — the SDK uses that to dedupe or stitch partials. The raw stream is best-effort for network issues, but the generation_id guarantees you can query the completed output later via rest endpoint, so UI can fallback to re-fetching the final text.

[00:03:46] Tom: From security POV — what about logs and PHI in transit for retries? Is the idempotency token exposing anything or is it opaque?
[00:03:54] Jordan: Tokens are opaque and not containing PHI. Retries are over TLS; for customers handling PHI, we recommend Private or Dedicated with customer-managed KMS and limited access to logs. We also support field-level redaction in audit logs as an add-on.

[00:04:10] Priya: Back to tuning: parameters that matter for latency/cost are max_tokens, temperature, top_p, and response_length heuristics. For short confirmations keep max_tokens low (20–60) and disable sampling if you want deterministic outputs — set temperature to 0. That reduces overall compute and tail latency.
[00:04:28] Amy: Are there built-in safety filters or content filters? We do some sanitization client-side.
[00:04:33] Priya: Yes there's a moderation endpoint and optional pre-filtering. For PHI workflows you can run a local prefilter to remove protected fields before sending, or use our redact SDK to mask fields.

[00:04:46] [00:04:46] Priya: Now quick demo of a retry scenario — I'll simulate a transient error by throttling the connection. (typing) The stream fails at ~10s; SDK detects and retries with exponential backoff by default (500ms, 1s, 2s).
[00:05:05] Priya: On a retry, if the generation is in our cache we return the final text quickly. If not, the retry will restart generation; the SDK will stitch or present the in-progress placeholder.
[00:05:18] Carlos: That backoff schedule is adjustable? We want more aggressive retries for low-latency UX.
[00:05:22] Priya: Yes it's configurable per-client. We advise careful tradeoff — too aggressive retries increase cost and may amplify load during an outage. We also support client-side circuit breakers that will stop retries after threshold.

[00:05:35] Samir: If a retry returns a slightly different completion due to sampling randomness, how do customers avoid showing inconsistent text to end users?
[00:05:42] Priya: Two approaches: 1) Use deterministic sampling (temperature=0) for idempotent outputs, or 2) keep the first successful completion and ignore subsequent retry responses if you have a stable generation_id. We can also store the canonical final response in a small per-conversation cache keyed by generation_id.

[00:05:58] Amy: For concurrency, if we have 200 concurrent users during peak, can hosted handle it? What's sizing guidance?
[00:06:06] Jordan: For Hosted we have scaling pools; throughput depends on model choice and prompt size. For short-turn traffic we recommend our dedicated small-instance model variants. We can run a micro-benchmark with your prompt set to estimate tokens/sec per slot and recommended concurrency per slot. That's what Priya will share.

[00:06:20] Priya: I'll drop into the Optimize UI — this shows suggested batching and quantization recommendations from historical traces. For example, if 80% of requests are under 120 tokens, Optimize suggests a smaller model variant and a 4k quantization that saves ~35% cost with minimal latency impact.
[00:06:38] Carlos: Nice. Is quantization available on hosted or only on Dedicated?
[00:06:42] Priya: Many quantized variants are available on hosted, but some extreme quant configs may only be on Dedicated. We'll indicate availability in the model catalog.

[00:06:51] [00:06:51] Priya: Quick note on fallbacks — we have multi-model policies. If preferred low-latency variant is saturated, requests can failover to a higher-latency but cheaper fallback. You can set SLOs (latency or cost) per route.
[00:07:05] Samir: What about consistency of behavior across failover? We need the UI to degrade gracefully, not break the conversation.
[00:07:11] Priya: Failover will attempt to pick a model with comparable instruction following; we recommend telling users there's a "brief delay" and showing a spinner. For critical flows, use Dedicated or reserve capacity.

[00:07:24] Carlos: Can we pin a model for specific routes? For example triage vs general chat?
[00:07:28] Jordan: Yes route-level model pinning is supported. That way critical routes use reserved capacity and others use shared pools.

[00:07:35] Amy: On SDKs — are there language bindings? We are Node + Python.
[00:07:39] Priya: Yes we have official Node and Python SDKs with built-in streaming handlers, plus examples for React streaming UI. The SDKs implement idempotency, retry policies, and chunk aggregation.

[00:07:50] Tom: Back to compliance — you mentioned audit logs. How long are logs retained and are they queryable?
[00:07:57] Jordan: Default retention is 30 days for hosted audit logs; can extend with add-on. Logs are queryable in the Console and can be exported to your SIEM. For PHI customers, longer retention and log redaction are common requests—we handle those via enterprise contract.

[00:08:12] Priya: I'm going to show a small QPS stress test in the console — I'm ramping to 100 qps with short prompt. (console noise) You can see token throughput, per-token latency histogram, and error rates. Right now this dev endpoint hits p95 of ~180ms with 100qps.
[00:08:30] Carlos: That's promising. How reproducible are these numbers? We need stable p95 across workdays.
[00:08:34] Priya: We'll run the micro-benchmark against the same hardware used in production. Results vary with model and region. We'll provide the benchmark script.

[00:08:42] Amy: Are there per-tenant throttles or is it elastically handled?
[00:08:46] Jordan: We do rate limiting to protect pools; you can set quotas per route. For bursty traffic we provide burst credits if configured ahead of time.

[00:08:56] [00:08:56] Priya: Quick walk-through of retry knobs in code snippet. (reads) Use requestId header, set max_retries, and use on_partial callback to handle streaming tokens. Example: set max_retries=3, backoff=[0.5,1,2], and clientBuffer=200ms to group deltas.
[00:09:16] Amy: The on_partial callback — do you recommend applying transforms client-side before render?
[00:09:20] Priya: Yes, do sanitization and dedupe client-side. The SDK includes helpers to filter out repeated whitespace tokens and token fragments.

[00:09:30] Carlos: If we start with Hosted and later migrate to Dedicated, how seamless is moving conversation state?
[00:09:36] Jordan: Conversation state persistence is your responsibility, but we provide export utilities and hooks for KV cache. Migration is mostly about re-routing the API keys and swapping model pins; we'll help with runbooks.

[00:09:47] Tom: Any SOC2 or pen-test reports you can share now?
[00:09:50] Jordan: Yes, I'll append the security pack link in follow-up: security_redwood_hc.pdf and SOC2-report-redwood.pdf. We'll redact anything needed.

[00:09:58] Priya: Quick live Q&A; Amy asked about partial tokens causing flicker. Two practical patterns: aggregate client updates every 100–300ms, or display incremental tokens but visually lock last committed sentence to avoid jumpiness.
[00:10:14] Samir: Nice. For voice readouts we might prefer earlier tokens; for text we want more stable sentences.

[00:10:22] [00:10:22] Priya: Showing a failure recovery flow: if the stream errored and retry returns a different output, SDK exposes generation_id — you can decide to keep first or adopt the last. For deterministic UIs keep the first successful final text.
[00:10:38] Carlos: What about cost calculations? Can you show a simple formula?
[00:10:42] Jordan: Sure — cost = (input tokens + output tokens) * per-token-rate. Optimize will estimate typical tokens per request and suggest model to hit cost target. We'll send an example spreadsheet.

[00:10:56] Amy: Any tips for reducing output tokens? We do confirmations for patients — short templates.
[00:11:00] Priya: Use instruction templates and placeholders, set max_tokens small, and prefer deterministic temperature=0. Also prefix caching reduces repeated context tokens.

[00:11:12] Tom: For auditability who can access the Console? We need RBAC and SSO.
[00:11:16] Jordan: We support SSO (SAML/OIDC) and fine-grained RBAC. You can restrict console access and API key scopes.

[00:11:24] [00:11:24] Priya: Wrapping up demo — live notes: p95 around 180ms in this run; backoff default shown; generation_id available for final fetch.
[00:11:34] Carlos: Great — can you send benchmark script and security docs?
[00:11:38] Jordan: Yes. Priya will drop the script; I'll send the security pack and pricing.

[00:11:44] Amy: One last question — is there a sandbox for us to test with PHI-like data?
[00:11:49] Jordan: We provide a sandbox but recommend you scrub real PHI; we can provide a VH (virtualized) dataset or partner with you on de-id tooling.

[00:11:58] Priya: Ok let's do quick recap and next steps.
[00:12:01] Jordan: Recap: Hosted can meet the latency target with appropriate model and config; streaming + retries handled by SDKs with idempotency and generation_id to reconcile; security features include KMS, audit logs, SSO, and private options. Action items: pricing, benchmark script, prompt set, security questions.
[00:12:17] Carlos: Thanks — we'll gather the prompt set and calendar a follow-up for the security review.

[00:12:24] [00:12:24] (some cross talk, call winding down)
[00:12:30] Jordan: Thanks everyone — we'll email the links.
[00:54:40] (call ends)

Notes on transcription: speaker labels are approximate; sometimes speaker turns are merged. References shared: security_redwood_hc.pdf (link), benchmark_script_v1.zip (link), pricing_tiers.xlsx (link).
